analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans import prescription drugs from Canada for personal use, in person or by mail.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up by the Senate committee that received it and died without any vote when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Department to write rules letting individuals bring prescription drugs from Canada in their luggage or order them by mail, so long as the drugs are for personal use, roughly a three-month supply, and come with information identifying the buyer and the treating doctor. It would also require the Secretary to study the safety of these imports and report to Congress. Because drugs in Canada often sell for far less than the same drugs in the United States, this would let patients buy their medicines at Canadian prices. The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles health matters and was never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill long-term prescriptions, especially seniors and people without good drug coverage, who could buy the same medicines in Canada at lower prices — a three-month personal supply, in their baggage or by mail.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People on long-term prescriptions, especially seniors

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write regulations permitting individuals to import prescription drugs from Canada for personal use, in personal baggage or by mail order.

Allows a personal supply such as a three-month supply, provided the buyer affirms it is for personal use, describes the product, and identifies the U.S.-licensed health professional responsible for the treatment.

Conditions importation on the product not posing a significant health risk, with that judgment made without any consideration of the drug's cost or availability in the United States — so price competition abroad cannot be used as a safety excuse.
Requires the Secretary to study the safety and purity of permitted imports and report to Congress within five years.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose some U.S. sales to lower-priced Canadian versions, and to a lesser extent U.S. pharmacies that would see some prescription purchases shift to Canadian mail order. Taxpayers fund the safety study and the regulatory program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug manufacturers and U.S. pharmacies

drawbacks.text: Drugs bought from Canadian sources are harder for regulators to verify: imported products can be mislabeled, substandard, or counterfeit, and personal-use shipments are less traceable than the domestic supply chain. The bill leaves it to the Secretary to set criteria 'to ensure the safety of patients,' so how much protection buyers actually got would depend entirely on the rules written after passage.

The bill addresses only the symptom of price gaps, not the cause: it limits imports to small personal quantities and does nothing about U.S. drug prices generally, so most patients would still face U.S. prices unless they went through the trouble of cross-border buying.

The buyer must identify a U.S.-licensed health professional responsible for the treatment or show the product continues a treatment begun abroad, adding paperwork that could be a barrier for some patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and direct: patients on maintenance medications could pay Canadian prices for the same pills. The cost is genuine but manageable in principle — safety risk from a less verifiable supply chain — and the bill leaves the safety guardrails to the Health and Human Services Secretary rather than writing them into law, which is both its flexibility and its weakness. The larger honest criticism is that it is a workaround, not a fix: it chips at the U.S.-Canada price gap for individual buyers without changing what Americans pay at home.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 1999, referred to the Senate health committee, and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim Jeffords of Vermont introduced the bill on July 29, 1999, to permit personal importation of prescription drugs from Canada in baggage or by mail order.
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That was the last action of any kind: the committee never reported the bill and the full Senate never voted on it, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: the U.S. market continued to pay American prices with no legal Canadian alternative, and the small cross-border buying that patients did stayed in a legal gray zone rather than becoming a protected right. The Senate committee is better off in the narrow sense that it never had to take a recorded position.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept U.S. prices

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 29, 1999 and gave introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Senate cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list shows one Republican cosponsor and no Democrats.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral for the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 29, 1999 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry broadly opposed drug reimportation legislation during this period, arguing imported drugs could not be guaranteed safe and that importation would erode U.S. sales at American prices.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only one sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, with no recorded votes, so no partisan split on the bill itself is visible; however, drug reimportation generally drew support from members of both parties who represented seniors and opposition from the pharmaceutical industry.

industries.note: The bill would open a legal channel for Americans to buy the same drugs at Canadian prices, cutting into U.S. sales priced far higher. The industry's interest in blocking importation ran directly against patients' savings.

Mail-order importation from Canada would become an expressly permitted channel, creating a legal market for cross-border prescription sales. Their gain comes from patients paying less, so their interest runs alongside buyers'.
Some prescription purchases would shift to Canadian sources, costing U.S. pharmacies sales, though they would remain the default channel for most fills.
